newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's LVMH buys prestigious Sauternes winemaker.
newsitem.headline: France's LVMH buys prestigious Sauternes winemaker.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH said on Thursday it was taking control of the acclaimed Chateau d'Yquem vineyard after striking a deal with most members of a feuding family that has held the property since 1785.

"It's a prestigious brand. It's a unique chateau," said a spokeswoman for LVMH, which added the elite Sauternes winemaker to a brand list that includes Moet & Chandon champagnes, Louis Vuitton luggage and Christian Dior perfumes.

LVMH said it concluded a deal on Thursday with several members of the Lur Saluces family to buy about 55 percent of the 113-hectare property, despite the opposition of Count Alexandre de Lur Saluces who manages it.
The chateau reacted angrily to the announcement, firing off a statement that the management was startled to hear of the agreement "and the manager himself knows nothing about it".
But investors applauded LVMH's move to add another prestige brand and drove the share price 1.1 percent higher at 1,284 francs on the Paris bourse.

The vineyard near Bordeaux in southwestern France is renowned for its sweet golden wines served with desserts and foie gras (fatted goose liver). Prices range from 600 francs ($115) for the 1987 vintage, a poor year, to more than 50,000 francs.

"Several members of the families associated with the Chateau d'Yquem have concluded an accord with LVMH. The Marquis (Eugene) de Lur-Saluces has joined the accord and an agreement has been established. Under the terms, LVMH is acquiring around 55 percent of Yquem," the company said in a statement.
The Marquis is Count Alexandre's brother.
The family feud at Chateau d'Yquem recalls a dispute at another LVMH target, California-based duty free chain DFS, whose partners are fighting over whether to sell to the French giant.
Chateau d'Yquem is the latest in a string of acquisitions, including Fred jewellers, Celine and Loewe luxury leather goods and a buyout of minority shareholders of Guerlain perfumes.
LVMH did not say how much it was paying for the controlling stake in Chateau d'Yquem, but an industry expert estimated the value of the entire property at one billion francs.

"(LVMH chairman) Bernard Arnault is buying himself a present," one analyst said. "It's a superb brand, it looks good in the portfolio, but this is clearly more of a purchase for pleasure than a strategically important acquisition."
Analyst Marie Laure Favre Gilly at Natwest Sellier said: "They can easily afford it."
Even with the acquisition of DFS for 12.6 billion francs -- currently under mediation in the United States -- LVMH's net gearing would be 37 percent which is quite manageable, she said.

Most analysts had not been briefed on details of the acquisition or the performance of Chateau d'Yquem, but some said LVMH may derive synergies between the Sauternes and cognac businesses, both of which are geared heavily to exports.
"They've certainly become more aggressive in acquisitions," said analyst Cecile d'Estais at Paribas Capital Markets. She did not expect Chateau d'Yquem marked the end of the buying spree.

Although the company's debt would surge from around three billion francs in June to nearly 17 billion if both the DFS and Chateau d'Yquem deals go through, d'Estais says the company has free cash flow of between two and 2.5 billion francs after capital expenditures, dividend payments and working capital.
Analysts shrugged off the internal disputes at the two target companies.

"A lot of luxury goods firms are family-owned and some family members want to sell, and some don't. If partners and relatives are fighting at DFS and Chateau d'Yquem, it's not LVMH's problem," one analyst said. ($ = 5.202 French Francs)
